problem: It says the trap instruction inside read() is privileged. A trap (system call) instruction is deliberately executable in user mode — that is the whole point of the controlled door. A privileged instruction is one the CPU refuses in user mode; if the trap instruction were privileged, no user program could ever make a system call. This contradicts Section 2 of the same chapter.
fix: Replace with: 'A privileged instruction is not "any important instruction". It is one the hardware blocks in user mode. read() is a library routine that puts a call number in registers and executes a trap instruction; the trap instruction itself is not privileged — it is the legal user-mode door into the kernel. What is privileged is everything the kernel does after the trap, such as setting the timer or masking interrupts.'

problem: Listing 'enter kernel mode' as an example of an instruction the CPU blocks in user mode clashes with Section 2, where entering kernel mode is exactly what a user program does through a trap. A student may conclude that a system call is forbidden in user mode.
fix: Say in Section 1: 'change the mode bit by a direct write' instead of 'enter kernel mode', and add one line: 'The hardware itself sets the mode bit to 0 when it takes a trap; the program cannot do it by writing the bit.' In Q5, drop 'enter kernel mode' from the accepted answers so they read: disable interrupts, set the timer, change the page-table base register, halt the CPU, do direct I/O.
